body:
Language, identity and state boundaries

When India became independent in 1947, the boundaries of most states largely reflected the administrative divisions created under British rule and the territories of former princely states. These boundaries did not always correspond to the languages spoken by the majority of their inhabitants.

The demand for linguistic states arose from the desire to organise administration and political representation around major regional languages. People believed that government working in their regional language would make administration more accessible and allow them to protect their linguistic and cultural identity.

The Indian National Congress had reorganised its own provincial committees largely on linguistic lines in 1920. However, after Partition in 1947, national leaders became cautious about immediately reorganising states on linguistic grounds. They feared that intense regional demands might weaken national unity. Administrative convenience, economic viability and national integration therefore remained important considerations.

Linguistic state

A linguistic state is a state whose territorial boundaries are organised substantially around a major language community. Language is an important basis for reorganisation, but administrative viability, economic considerations and national unity must also be considered.

The Andhra precedent and the States Reorganisation Commission

The demand for linguistic states gained strength through the movement for a separate Telugu-speaking state. Potti Sriramulu undertook a fast demanding a separate state for Telugu-speaking people. He died on 15 December 1952 after his fast, leading to widespread protests.

The Government of India consequently created Andhra State on 1 October 1953, separating the Telugu-speaking areas from Madras State. This was an important precedent for other linguistic movements.

On 1 November 1956, after the merger of additional Telugu-speaking territories from Hyderabad State, Andhra State became Andhra Pradesh. Therefore, Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956) should not be treated as identical territorial arrangements.

To examine the wider demand for reorganising Indian states, the Government of India appointed the States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) in 1953.

PositionName
ChairmanFazl Ali
MemberH.N. Kunzru
MemberK.M. Panikkar

The Commission submitted its report in 1955. It accepted language as an important basis for reorganising states but did not treat language as the only consideration. National unity, administrative efficiency and economic viability also mattered.

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956

Parliament enacted the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 on 31 August 1956. Its appointed day was 1 November 1956. The reorganisation resulted in 14 states and 6 Union Territories.

The Act also created a new and enlarged Bombay State. Its territory included the earlier Bombay State (excluding Bijapur, Dharwar and Kanara districts, Belgaum district except Chandgad taluka, and Abu Road taluka of Banaskantha district), the former states of Saurashtra and Kutch, the Marathi-speaking region of Vidarbha from Madhya Pradesh and the Marathi-speaking region of Marathwada from Hyderabad State.

Consequently, the enlarged Bombay State contained two major linguistic communities: Gujarati-speaking people and Marathi-speaking people. It came to be known as the bilingual Bombay State.

The important distinction

The 1956 reorganisation did not create a separate Gujarat. It brought Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking regions together in one enlarged Bombay State. The demand for separate Gujarat continued.

Prelims focus

  • Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953 following the movement associated with Potti Sriramulu.
  • The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in 1953 under Fazl Ali.
  • The SRC submitted its report in 1955.
  • The States Reorganisation Act, 1956, came into effect on 1 November 1956.
  • The 1956 reorganisation resulted in 14 states and 6 Union Territories.
  • Trap: Andhra State was formed in 1953; Andhra Pradesh emerged in 1956. Gujarat was formed separately only in 1960.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, pp. 21–23; NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts–III, Chapter 10, India After Independence, pp. 134–135; The States Reorganisation Act, 1956, sections 1–2 and 8, India Code (consulted 22 November 2026).]

title: Linguistic Reorganisation and the Bilingual Bombay State

body:
Why the movement began

The Mahagujarat movement was a political and popular movement demanding a separate state for Gujarati-speaking people out of the enlarged bilingual Bombay State. Its central objective was to bring the Gujarati-speaking territories together under a separate state government.

The movement gained strength because the 1956 reorganisation had not created a separate Gujarat. Instead, Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking regions had been combined in one large Bombay State. Many Gujarati-speaking people feared that their political representation, regional interests and linguistic identity would receive inadequate attention within the composite state.

The demand was not merely about language. It also involved regional political representation, control over administration and the economic interests connected with Bombay city, which was an important centre of trade and commerce.

The turning point of August 1956

A proposed three-unit arrangement involving separate Gujarat, Maharashtra and Bombay city as a distinct unit was withdrawn in August 1956. Parliament instead accepted the creation of a large bilingual Bombay State. This sudden reversal generated strong opposition in Gujarat.

On 8 August 1956, a large group of students marched towards Congress House in Ahmedabad to protest against the decision. The situation became violent, and police firing killed and injured some students. Demonstrations and police firing also occurred in places such as Kalol and Nadiad.

The deaths of students generated widespread public sympathy for the demand for Mahagujarat. The agitation consequently developed beyond its initial student participation into a wider political movement.

Student leadership and political organisation

Harihar Khambholja, a law student, led the student organisation that emerged during the agitation. The students formed the Maha Gujarat Vidyarthi Samiti, which played an important role in the initial phase of the movement.

In September 1956, a citizens' convention known as the Nagrik Parishad was held in Ahmedabad. Nearly 1,000 delegates from different parts of Gujarat participated. The convention brought different political and social groups together under the wider political organisation called the Mahagujarat Janata Parishad (MGJP).

Indulal Yagnik was elected president of the Mahagujarat Janata Parishad. He became the principal political leader associated with the movement and played a prominent role in organising the demand for a separate Gujarat.

Person or organisationRole in the movement
Indulal YagnikPresident and principal political leader of the Mahagujarat Janata Parishad.
Harihar KhambholjaStudent leader associated with the Maha Gujarat Vidyarthi Samiti.
Maha Gujarat Vidyarthi SamitiStudent organisation active during the initial agitation.
Mahagujarat Janata ParishadWider political organisation campaigning for a separate Gujarat.

The dispute over Bombay city

Bombay city was a major point of disagreement between the Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking movements. The Mahagujarat Janata Parishad demanded a separate Gujarat comprising Gujarati-speaking areas and also claimed Bombay city. The parallel Samyukta Maharashtra movement demanded a separate Marathi-speaking Maharashtra that included Bombay city.

Bombay city had a diverse population and strong commercial connections with Gujarat as well as Maharashtra. Its future therefore became an important part of the political negotiations over the division of Bombay State.

MovementMain demandPosition on Bombay city
Mahagujarat movementSeparate state for Gujarati-speaking areas.The Mahagujarat Janata Parishad included Bombay city in its demand.
Samyukta Maharashtra movementSeparate state for Marathi-speaking areas.Demanded Bombay city as part of Maharashtra.
Final settlement, 1960Separate Gujarat and Maharashtra.Bombay city became part of Maharashtra.

The response of the central leadership

On 1 October 1956, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru addressed people at Rajkot. He acknowledged the shock, frustration and anger caused in Gujarat by the sudden decision to form the larger Bombay State. He also expressed sympathy for the families affected by police firing. At the same time, he emphasised the importance of national unity and cautioned against allowing linguistic demands to create hostility between regions.

The movement continued through political organisation, public demonstrations and electoral participation. Ultimately, the demand for separate Gujarat was accepted through the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.

Prelims focus

  • 8 August 1956: student protest at Congress House, Ahmedabad.
  • Harihar Khambholja was associated with the Maha Gujarat Vidyarthi Samiti.
  • Indulal Yagnik was elected president of the Mahagujarat Janata Parishad.
  • The Nagrik Parishad convention brought nearly 1,000 delegates together in Ahmedabad in September 1956.
  • The Mahagujarat and Samyukta Maharashtra movements both had claims concerning Bombay city.
  • Trap: Bombay city became part of Maharashtra in 1960, not Gujarat.

[Sources: Bharti Pradyot Kansara, Business, Labour and Opposition Movements in the Politics of Ahmedabad City, 1900–72, PhD thesis, University of London, 1975, pp. 32–34; The Nehru Archive, Mahagujerat Janata Parishad organisation record; Jawaharlal Nehru, Pathway to Progress, speech at Rajkot, 1 October 1956 (consulted 22 November 2026).]

title: The Mahagujarat Movement: Organisation, Leaders and Demands

body:
The legal division of Bombay State

The demand for a separate Gujarat ultimately resulted in the division of the bilingual Bombay State. Parliament enacted the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, officially designated as Act No. 11 of 1960.

The Act received assent on 25 April 1960 and defined 1 May 1960 as the appointed day. From this date, a new state called Gujarat was formed. The remaining territory of the former Bombay State became the State of Maharashtra.

Formation date

Gujarat and Maharashtra became separate states on 1 May 1960 under the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.

The original territorial composition of Gujarat

Section 3 of the Act specified the territories that formed the new State of Gujarat. It included 17 districts of the former Bombay State:

Banaskantha, Mehsana, Sabarkantha, Ahmedabad, Kaira (now Kheda), Panchmahals, Baroda (now Vadodara), Broach (now Bharuch), Surat, Dangs, Amreli, Surendranagar, Rajkot, Jamnagar, Junagadh, Bhavnagar and Kutch.

The Act also transferred certain specified villages from Umbergaon taluka of Thana district and from Nawapur, Nandurbar, Akkalkuwa and Taloda talukas of West Khandesh district. These were specified village-level territorial transfers; the entire talukas were not transferred to Gujarat.

The residuary Bombay State was renamed Maharashtra. Bombay city, now known as Mumbai, remained in Maharashtra. Thus, although Bombay city had been an important part of the Mahagujarat demand, it was not included in the newly formed Gujarat State.

Initial representation in legislatures

The Bombay Reorganisation Act also determined the initial representation of the two new states in Parliament and their legislative assemblies.

InstitutionInitial Gujarat allocation
Rajya Sabha11 seats
Lok Sabha22 seats
Gujarat Legislative Assembly132 directly elected seats

The Act provided that the strength of the Gujarat Legislative Assembly would increase from 132 to 154 after the expiry of the first Assembly's term or its dissolution. These are historical initial allocations, not the present strengths of the institutions.

Separate constitutional institutions

The Act provided for a separate Gujarat High Court from the appointed day. The Bombay High Court became the High Court for Maharashtra. This gave Gujarat its own High Court instead of continuing under the jurisdiction of the Bombay High Court.

Dr Jivraj Mehta became the first Chief Minister of Gujarat. Ahmedabad initially served as the capital of the newly formed state. The later development of Gandhinagar as the new capital is an important part of Gujarat's early administrative history.

Remember the two stages

1 November 1956: the enlarged bilingual Bombay State was formed.
1 May 1960: the bilingual Bombay State was divided into Gujarat and Maharashtra.

Prelims focus

  • Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960: Act No. 11 of 1960.
  • 25 April 1960: date of the Act.
  • 1 May 1960: appointed day and formation of Gujarat and Maharashtra.
  • Gujarat was initially formed from 17 districts and specified border villages.
  • Gujarat initially received 11 Rajya Sabha seats, 22 Lok Sabha seats and 132 Assembly seats.
  • Dr Jivraj Mehta was the first Chief Minister of Gujarat.
  • Trap: Bombay city remained in Maharashtra, not Gujarat.

[Sources: The Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 (Act No. 11 of 1960), sections 2–3, 6, 10, 13 and 28, India Code (consulted 22 November 2026); Yojana, May 2021, Growth Story of Gujarat, p. 13 (consulted 22 November 2026).]
